title: Mechanisms of Prompt-Induced Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
text: A substantial body of work has investigated hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) Ji et al. ( 2023 ); Tonmoy et al. ( 2024 ); Huang et al. ( 2025 ) . Prior work has shown that hallucinations can be reliably induced through out-of-distribution prompting Yao et al. ( 2023 ) , long context windows Li et al. ( 2024b ); Xu et al. ( 2024a ) , or the use of explicit personas Joshi et al. ( 2024 ); Simhi et al. ( 2025 ) . However, these settings often reflect adversarial or non-realistic usage patterns, rather than the models’ behavior under typical user interactions. Previous studies have demonstrated that LLMs may produce incorrect outputs when prompts contradict internal knowledge Xie et al. ( 2023 ); Xu et al. ( 2024b ) or contain errors subsequently repeated or amplified by the model Zhang et al. ( 2023b ); Simhi et al. ( 2025 ) . This behavior has been linked to cognitive-like biases, including anchoring bias, where models rely disproportionately on information introduced in the prompt Jones and Steinhardt ( 2022 ); Echterhoff et al. ( 2024 ); Malberg et al. ( 2025 ) , and sycophancy, where models conform to user assumptions despite conflicting evidence Sharma et al. ( 2024 ) . Vision–language models (VLMs) integrate textual and visual information, introducing additional complexity.
